title: The Trench
hook: Salman's trench, the whole city digging on a cold morning, a rock that breaks, and Jabir's small meal that feeds the diggers (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahd, and the hardest chapter on this stretch of the path. Your line was: hard history, told honestly.

A cold morning, and the sound of picks on stony ground. A great army of allied tribes is coming for Medina. The biographers say the plan came from Salman the Persian: dig a trench across the open side of the city. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Anas describes the Muhajirun and the Ansar, the people of Mecca and the people of Medina, digging in the cold with no servants to do it for them. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ comes out and sees how tired and hungry they are. Today: the Trench.
screen: `A COLD MORNING.` → `SALMAN'S PLAN.` → `NO SERVANTS TO DIG FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: What he does first is sing with them. In Anas's report, he calls out a line of verse: O Allah, the real life is the life of the Hereafter, so forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirun. The diggers call back: we are the ones who pledged to Muhammad, to strive as long as we live. A call and an answer, across a ditch. Al-Bara, also in Bukhari, adds that the Prophet carried earth himself until the dust covered his belly, reciting the verses of the poet Abdullah ibn Rawahah: without You, O Allah, we would not have been guided, nor given charity, nor prayed, so send calm down on us and make our feet firm. Firm feet: the same gift as the night rain before Badr. Then the rock. Jabir says they hit a rock no one could break. The Prophet took the pick and struck, and it fell apart into loose sand. An-Nasa'i's Sunan tells of three strikes, each throwing off a flash of light. Then Jabir tells something smaller and lovelier. Seeing the Prophet's hunger, he slipped home. His wife had a little barley and a young goat; they cooked it, and Jabir quietly invited the Prophet with one or two others. Instead the Prophet called out to the whole trench: Jabir has made a meal, come on! Jabir's wife, worried, asked if the Prophet knew how little there was. He did. In Jabir's telling, everyone ate their fill, and the pot was still bubbling. Many hands, one trench, one pot.
screen: `A CALL AND AN ANSWER, ACROSS A DITCH.` · `DUST ON HIS BELLY, FEET MADE FIRM.` · `THE ROCK FALLS INTO SAND.` · `JABIR'S SMALL MEAL FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `DIG TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Think of a shared job ahead, at work or after a family meal, and notice where you usually stand: in front giving directions, off to the side, or not there at all. Picture yourself in the ditch with everyone else, carrying earth, noticing who's tired and who's hungry, and what small thing you could bring, like Jabir's pot. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless the work.
The Trench: Salman's plan, dug by the people of Mecca and Medina together in the cold, with the Prophet carrying earth and singing beside them. Today's word.
Your line: dig together. He carried the earth too, until the dust covered him. Day seven hundred eighty-two, done.

howItsDone: The Battle of the Trench, al-Khandaq, is taught in sirah classes, and the diggers' call and answer from Sahih al-Bukhari is sometimes recited as an example of the Prophet working alongside his companions.

original.note: Arabic: the trench; the battle is called the Battle of the Trench, and also of the Confederates, al-Ahzab.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ditch that stopped an army.
what it means: a city that dug together, sang together, and ate from one pot.
what a scholar hears: Anas's call and answer, Ibn Rawahah's verses in al-Bara's report, and Jabir's rock and meal.

chat.says: What did the Prophet do while his companions dug the trench?
options: He dug and carried earth with them, singing, and shared Jabir's meal.
He stood back and directed, since leaders didn't do the digging.
He stayed in the mosque, praying for the diggers until they finished.
chat.meaning: Al-Bara says he carried earth until dust covered his belly; Anas tells of the call and answer, and Jabir of the meal that fed the trench.

Salman the Persian.meaning: a companion from Persia, credited with the trench plan

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2834 (Anas: the Muhajirun and Ansar digging on a cold morning with no servants; the call and answer)

Ibn Sa'd, at-Tabaqat al-Kubra; al-Waqidi, al-Maghazi (Salman's suggestion of the trench)

notes: The index cites Bukhari for 'a rock broken with three strikes'. Bukhari 4101 (Jabir) has the rock crumbling to sand without a count; the three strikes with flashes of light are in an-Nasa'i (and Ahmad). The script tells both and attributes each; confirm an-Nasa'i 3176 and consider correcting the index.
Salman's suggestion comes from the sirah (Ibn Sa'd, al-Waqidi), not Bukhari; framed as 'the biographers say'.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm Bukhari 2834, 4101, 4102, 4104.
The verses of the call and answer and Ibn Rawahah's lines are paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the sense.
Jabir's wife's question is from Bukhari 4101 / 4102; the versions differ slightly in what she says; confirm 'asked if the Prophet knew how little there was'.
Bukhari 4102 gives a number of diggers who ate; omitted under the claims rule.
'Firm feet: the same gift as the night rain before Badr' links Ibn Rawahah's verse to 8:11 (day 776); confirm the link is fair.
Day 268 (year 1) covered Salman's idea and the stone of hunger, and year 2 day 539 the rock; this day centers on the call and answer and Jabir's meal.
The practice describes asking for blessing in general terms, not a new prayer.
